segments: 214 Chronography of Barhebraeus.
silver coins and gold dinars,
and vessels of gold and of silver, and noble garments,
and an abundance of mules,
so that a choice mule was sold in Aleppo for two dinars.
It is said
that not even a single tent-cloth,
or a cup to drink water with, escaped with that Romanus.
And at this time, Romanus, the king of the Romans, died suddenly,
and Michael reigned after him.
And there rose up against him a certain base man of his family whose name was Kalaphates (Michael V).
And when that rebel Kalaphates had stood for five months,
he was seized,
and both of his eyes were put out.
And in the year 422 {AH},
For he was virtuous and chaste,
and not dissolute like those who were before him.
And there arose after him Abu Ja'far his son,
and he was called al-Qa'im.
After al-Qadir, al-Qa'im {OCR?} reigned for forty-four years and eight months.
To him all the Persian, Turkish, and Arab nobles readily submitted,
and they gave the hand of oaths (swore allegiance).
Now the Turks, when according to custom they demanded the gift of the renewal of the reign,
and there was nothing in the treasury of the Caliph—
because the Persian emirs had dominion over all the lands,
even over Baghdad,
and only pensions were being given to the Caliph—
the Caliph al-Qa'im sold an inn and gardens and something from the treasures of his palace,
and gave it to them, and they were quieted.
At this time, when two Arab emirs were ruling in Edessa,
Ibn 'Utayr and Ibn Shibab,
each one in a fortress,
Ibn 'Utayr sent to Michael {OCR?}, king of the Romans,
and sold him his fortress for twenty thousand darics and four villages in the Roman territory.
And the Romans came by night,
and took control and entered into the fortress, and fortified themselves in it,
because it was like a citadel.
And some of them went down into the city,
and destroyed the mosque of the Arabs.
And when Nasir al-Dawla heard,
he sent an army against Edessa, and they conquered it,
and breached its wall and entered it.
And they also took the Great Church, to which the Christians had fled,
and plundered them and their women.
And they attacked again the fortress of the Romans,
and were not able to approach it,
notes: 422 of the Arabs: al-Qadir, the Caliph of Baghdad, died at the age of eighty-seven years.
